templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Items in a series (commas; semicolons when items contain commas)
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation inside a compound joined by and
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between subject and verb
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a prepositional phrase
items.passage: Discovered on a mummified woman’s foot in a Theban tomb, the Cairo toe is a prosthetic big toe, crafted from wood and leather, that is nearly three thousand years ______ a 2011 experiment, two volunteers lacking their right big toes walked comfortably in replica sandals while wearing a reconstruction.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Discovered ... nearly three thousand years old” is a complete sentence, and so is “In a 2011 experiment, two volunteers ... walked comfortably ... while wearing a reconstruction.” The period after “old” correctly separates the two; “In a 2011 experiment” introduces the second sentence, whose subject is “two volunteers.”

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses; “old, in a 2011 experiment, two volunteers ... walked” is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the clauses run together, and “in a 2011 experiment” wrongly seems to say when the toe was three thousand years old.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, “and” can't be used to join these two long independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: history (ancient Egyptian medicine). Band 6 as planned: a 4-word opener before clause 2’s subject (“In a 2011 experiment, two volunteers”), the 2.10 / 67667d72 move with a different menu (no “which”). No semicolon option, which would be a second correct answer. Facts kept to what is well established (Theban tomb, wood and leather, about 950 to 710 BCE, 2011 replica tests with two volunteers); researchers unnamed.

review.note: Draft notes corrected: the opener is 4 words to the subject, not 8 (item text unchanged).

band7.why: Target 6. S1_period on 67667d72 (2.10, band 6): opener “In a 2011 experiment,” is 4 words to the subject, under the band-6 median of 8 but inside the band-6 range; splice, fused and and-without-comma menu.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a participial phrase
items.passage: Ball lightning, a luminous sphere observed during thunderstorms, is too rare and fleeting for systematic study. In 2012, however, researchers monitoring ordinary lightning on China’s Qinghai Plateau unexpectedly captured one with their ______ the spectrum of the sphere’s brief glow, they identified silicon, iron, and calcium, elements abundant in soil.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The first clause, “In 2012, however, researchers ... captured one with their spectrographs,” is complete. “Analyzing the spectrum of the sphere’s brief glow” is a participial phrase that describes “they,” the subject of the next main clause (“they identified silicon, iron, and calcium”). A period after “spectrographs” correctly makes these two separate sentences.

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “analyzing the spectrum of the sphere’s brief glow” look like a modifier of the first clause, but “they identified ...” is a second independent clause, so the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “spectrographs analyzing the spectrum ...” reads as one noun phrase, and the two independent clauses are fused.

D.why_wrong: Adding “that” starts a relative clause that never gets a verb of its own; “they identified ...” then follows a comma, leaving a confused, ungrammatical sentence.

items.notes: Subject: science (atmospheric physics). Band 6: a 4-word participial opener (b15724fc “Praising”, 3.4 “By dissolving”) that can hang on “spectrographs” in A and B until “they identified” arrives. The 2012 Qinghai observation of ball lightning's spectrum (silicon, iron, calcium) is described without naming the researchers.

fixes: lengthened the opener of the second sentence from 3 to 7 words (“Analyzing the spectrum of the sphere’s brief glow”) so the splice in A and B surfaces 8 words after the blank, as in the band-6 models b15724fc and 1b97cce9; explanation and why_wrong updated
dropped “occasionally” from the context sentence to keep the passage near the models’ length (49 words)

band7.why: Target 6. After the fix the participial opener runs 7 words and could hang on “spectrographs” in A and B until “they identified” arrives 8 words past the blank (b15724fc, 1b97cce9 shape); D adds “that,” (added-word recipe).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a long adjective phrase that could modify the first clause's last noun
items.passage: In 1974, Nigerian modernist Ben Enwonwu painted Adetutu Ademiluyi, a Yoruba princess, in three ______ for decades and familiar to most Nigerians only through reproductions, one of these paintings resurfaced in a London apartment in 2017, and its 2018 auction price exceeded a million pounds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 1974, ... Ben Enwonwu painted Adetutu Ademiluyi, a Yoruba princess, in three portraits” is a complete sentence. The phrase “Missing for decades and familiar to most Nigerians only through reproductions” describes “one of these paintings,” the subject of the next sentence, so a period must come after “portraits.”

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “missing for decades ...” seems to describe the portraits in the first clause, but “one of these paintings resurfaced ...” is a second independent clause, so the sentence is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “portraits missing for decades ...” glues the phrase to the first clause, and the comma before “one of these paintings” then joins two independent clauses: a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: “That were missing ...” turns the phrase into a relative clause about the portraits, but “one of these paintings resurfaced ...” still follows with only a comma, producing a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Nigerian modernist painting). Band-7 checks: the opener is an 11-word adjective phrase (“Missing for decades and familiar to most Nigerians only through reproductions”) that reads naturally as a modifier of “portraits” in A, B and C (the 3.8 and 4b424102 move, with a new opener type); clause 2's subject arrives 13 words after the blank, outside a 6-word window; the run is the whole 45-word passage; reasoning steps 3. Added-word option as in 4b424102 (“who are known”).
band7_moves: opener of 11 words that can modify the first clause's last noun (portraits)
clause 2's subject arrives 13 words after the blank
two comma-splice disguises (bare comma, “that were”) plus the glued form

review.note: Enwonwu: three Tutu portraits, 2017 London rediscovery and 2018 sale are his standard record; kept.

band7.why: S1_period on 4b424102 and 3.8: an 11-word adjective opener reads as a modifier of “portraits” in A, B and C; clause 2’s subject comes 13 words past the blank; added-word option as 4b424102; no option is killed by a local cue.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opening the second clause (rather), semicolon before it
items.passage: In 1909, Japanese poet Ishikawa Takuboku kept a diary he was determined to conceal from his wife. To guarantee its confidentiality, he did not devise a secret ______ he composed the diary in rōmaji, a romanized transcription of Japanese that he believed his wife could not read.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “To guarantee its confidentiality, he did not devise a secret code” and “he composed the diary in rōmaji ...” are both independent clauses. The semicolon after “code” correctly joins them, and “rather,” which introduces what Takuboku did instead, belongs at the start of the second clause, set off by a comma.

B.why_wrong: Commas around “rather” can't join two independent clauses; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation after “code,” the two independent clauses run together.

D.why_wrong: Placing the semicolon after “rather” attaches the adverb to the first clause, but “rather” must introduce the alternative (writing in rōmaji), so it can't close the clause that states what he did not do.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Japanese poetry, Meiji era). Band 6 on 3.5 (a9e5b788): “not X; rather, Y.” Menu adds the misplaced “, rather;” in place of 3.5's bare-comma option. No period option (“code. Rather, he ...” would be a second correct answer). Hedged “he believed his wife could not read,” since accounts differ on what Setsuko could read.

fixes: removed “neither hid the notebook nor”: a detail about a real person not in the record; the clause now says only that he did not devise a secret code
review.note: Takuboku: rōmaji diary of 1909 kept from his wife is the standard record; the added detail was removed.

band7.why: Target 6. “; rather,” opening clause 2 is the band-6 adverb shape (a9e5b788, 3.5); band-7 adverb keys close clause 1 with though or however.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closing clause 1 (contrast with the previous sentence), semicolon after it
items.passage: Over millions of years, bombardment by the solar wind, a stream of charged particles from the Sun, gradually darkens exposed lunar soil. The pale, looping markings called lunar swirls have largely escaped this ______ magnetic fields preserved in the underlying crust apparently deflect the incoming particles.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The previous sentence says the solar wind darkens exposed lunar soil, and the clause “The pale, looping markings ... have largely escaped this darkening” runs against that, so “though” belongs at the end of this clause, set off by a comma. The semicolon after “though” then joins the clause to the next one, “magnetic fields ... apparently deflect the incoming particles,” which explains why the swirls have escaped the darkening.

A.why_wrong: After the semicolon, “though” would begin a dependent clause (“though magnetic fields ... deflect the incoming particles”), and a semicolon can't join a main clause to a dependent clause.

B.why_wrong: With a period, “Though magnetic fields preserved in the underlying crust apparently deflect the incoming particles” would stand alone as a sentence, but “though” makes it a dependent clause with no main clause: a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Commas alone can't join the two independent clauses; the comma after “though” creates a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (lunar geology). Band-7 checks: the adverb closes clause 1, which contrasts with the previous sentence (the solar wind darkens lunar soil); clause 2 explains clause 1, so B's concessive “though” fails only on meaning, the cue sitting in the previous sentence; A and D fail on rule. Menu of 5aa171de and 790fc366. Run 24 words (as 21e58a83 and b771d175, both band 7 with short runs).
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, which runs against the previous sentence
logic-wrong distractor (concessive “though”) is grammatical and fails only on meaning
clause 2 explains clause 1, so no concession reading survives

review.safety_fix: safety solve found B (', though' as a subordinator) grammatical and wrong only on meaning, defensible to a careful student; B is now '. Though', a fragment, wrong by rule

band7.why: after the safety fix every wrong option fails on a punctuation rule; the logic-only trap that made it band 7 is gone

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause ending in a stranded preposition, before the specified item
items.passage: Although navigators of Micronesia’s Caroline Islands interpret swells, clouds, and seabird movements to cross vast expanses of ocean without instruments, there is one system that apprentices concentrate most ______ the star compass, a ring of points on the horizon where particular stars rise and set.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause “there is one system that apprentices concentrate most intensively on” is complete (the relative clause ends with its preposition, “on”). A colon after “on” correctly introduces the noun phrase that names that system: “the star compass, a ring of points on the horizon ....”

A.why_wrong: The period separates the preposition “on” from the clause it belongs to and leaves “On the star compass, a ring of points ...” as a fragment.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join the main clause to “the star compass ...,” a noun phrase rather than an independent clause.

C.why_wrong: Without a colon, “the star compass” becomes a second object of “on,” whose object is already “that”; the sentence is ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: social science (navigation and traditional knowledge, Micronesia). Band 6 on fba5d8d1 (“high on:”): the clause ends in a stranded preposition, so the period and no-mark options look natural. No comma or lone-dash option: either could be defended before an appositive-like specified item.

band7.why: Target 6. fba5d8d1 frame and menu (stranded preposition, then a colon before the named item).

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that contains finite verbs in relative clauses
items.passage: During the Prussian siege of Paris in 1870 and 1871, balloons transported mail out of the city but could not be navigated back in. Correspondence reached Parisians by an older ______ pigeons that carried, rolled inside a quill, transparent films on which photographer René Dagron had reduced thousands of dispatches to microscopic size.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Correspondence reached Parisians by an older means” is a complete clause that announces a means without naming it. A colon after “means” correctly introduces the noun phrase that names it: “homing pigeons that carried ... transparent films on which ... Dagron had reduced thousands of dispatches to microscopic size.” That phrase has no main verb of its own (“carried” and “had reduced” are inside relative clauses).

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “by an older means homing pigeons” runs the noun phrase into the clause and is ungrammatical.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two independent clauses, but “homing pigeons that carried ...” is a noun phrase with no main verb.

D.why_wrong: The period leaves “Homing pigeons that carried ... to microscopic size” as a fragment: its verbs belong to relative clauses, and the phrase has no main verb.

items.notes: Subject: history (siege of Paris, 1870 to 1871). Band-7 checks: the specified item is a 29-word noun phrase whose relative clauses carry finite verbs (“carried,” “had reduced”), so the semicolon and period options look as if they introduce a sentence (the 3.18 and 3.26 move); the announcing phrase is a bare noun (“an older means”), unlike e9aee0d8's comparative. Menu as f30a478e (none, colon, semicolon, period). No comma or lone dash offered.
band7_moves: specified item is a long noun phrase whose relative clauses carry finite verbs
period and semicolon options look like they start a sentence until the reader finds no main verb
the deciding check (no main verb) sits 20+ words after the blank

fixes: explanation quoted “thin films”; the passage says “transparent films”
review.note: Dagron: microfilm pigeon post in the 1870 to 1871 siege is the standard record; kept.

band7.why: f30a478e menu (none, colon, semicolon, period); the specified noun phrase runs 29 words with finite verbs inside relative clauses (“carried”, “had reduced”), so the semicolon and period read as if a sentence follows (3.18, 3.26 move).

items.subtype: Restrictive title and name inside a participial phrase whose closing comma follows the name
items.passage: By the 1940s, Manx, the Celtic language traditionally spoken on the Isle of Man, retained only a few elderly native speakers. Recordings of their speech, made in 1948 by the Irish Folklore Commission with speakers such as ______ proved indispensable to revivalists after Maddrell died in 1974.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Fisherman Ned Maddrell” is a title plus a name; the name identifies which fisherman is meant, so no comma separates them. The comma after “Maddrell” is needed for a different reason: it closes the phrase “made in 1948 by the Irish Folklore Commission with speakers such as fisherman Ned Maddrell,” which was opened by the comma after “speech.” The subject “Recordings of their speech” then takes its verb, “proved.”

B.why_wrong: The comma between “fisherman” and “Ned Maddrell” treats the name as extra information, but it is essential to identifying the fisherman, so no punctuation belongs there.

C.why_wrong: The phrase that begins “made in 1948” was opened with a comma after “speech,” so it needs a closing comma after “Maddrell” before the verb “proved.”

D.why_wrong: This option both separates the title from the name with a comma and omits the comma that must close the phrase beginning “made in 1948.”

items.notes: Subject: language (Manx revival, Isle of Man). Band-7 checks: two slots, each a different rule (title plus name with no comma; the partner comma that closes a supplement opened 14 words earlier), the second-slot move of 0a114526 with a partner comma instead of a quotation; the descriptor is article-less (“fisherman”), so the comma pair in B cannot be defended as a nonrestrictive appositive. Run 31 words.
band7_moves: title plus name with a second slot governed by a different rule
the second slot's cue (the opening comma after “speech”) is 14 words before the blank
commas around the name look polite but the descriptor is article-less

review.note: Irish Folklore Commission 1948 Manx recordings and Ned Maddrell (fisherman, died 1974) are the standard record; kept.

band7.why: Title plus name with a second slot governed by a different rule: the partner comma of a phrase opened 14 words earlier (0a114526, 5aae2475, 59a246dc shape); the article-less descriptor rules out B.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses; the second opens with a prepositional phrase
items.passage: Known only from fossils until its 1994 discovery in a remote Australian canyon, the Wollemi pine survives in the wild as fewer than 100 mature ______ during the catastrophic bushfires of 2019–2020, firefighters protected their grove with an irrigation system.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Known only from fossils ..., the Wollemi pine survives in the wild as fewer than 100 mature trees” and “during the catastrophic bushfires of 2019–2020, firefighters protected their grove with an irrigation system” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses, even though “during the catastrophic bushfires” makes the comma look like it sets off a phrase.

items.notes: Subject: science (botany, conservation). Plan asked band 6; S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items. Strong band 6 on 7ce4ee13 and 3.9: clause 2 opens with an 8-word time phrase, so the bare comma (C) looks like it sets off a phrase before the subject. Both clauses are long, so the comma-less “and” is wrong by CB's own rationale. No semicolon or period option.

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on the 7ce4ee13 menu with an 8-word time phrase opening clause 2.

items.subtype: Semicolons between items of a complex series; second slot sets off a supplement inside item 2
items.passage: During a nine-month experiment at Ctrip, a Chinese travel agency, call-center employees randomly assigned to telecommute took fewer breaks and sick days, which increased their working ______ probably because home was quieter than the office; and resigned at half the rate of office-based colleagues.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The sentence lists three things the employees did, and each item contains its own commas, so semicolons separate the items, as the semicolon after “office” shows. A semicolon is therefore needed after “time,” and the comma after “faster” is needed to set off “probably because home was quieter than the office,” which explains why they worked faster.

A.why_wrong: A comma after “time” fails to match the semicolon that separates the second and third items, so the boundary between the first two items is unclear.

B.why_wrong: A colon can't be used between two items of a series.

D.why_wrong: The semicolon after “faster” cuts “probably because home was quieter than the office” off from the item it explains, making it look like a separate item in the series.

items.notes: Subject: social science (economics of remote work; the 2010 to 2011 Ctrip experiment, researchers unnamed). Band-7 checks: item 1 carries an internal comma (“, which increased their working time”); the revealing semicolon comes 10 words after the blank; the option holds a second slot governed by a different rule (the comma before item 2's supplement), the 9c3630b9 move. Run is the whole 44-word sentence.
band7_moves: blank in item 1, revealing semicolon after the blank
second slot in the option tests a different rule (comma before a supplement)
item 1 carries its own comma-set relative clause

review.note: Ctrip: the real telecommuting experiment, researchers unnamed; kept.

band7.why: 9c3630b9 and aaa1907f shape: item 1 holds a comma, the revealing semicolon comes 10 words after the blank, and the option carries a second slot governed by a different rule (comma before “probably because”).

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing absolute phrase whose noun carries a finite relative clause
items.passage: The Tabula Peutingeriana, a medieval reproduction of an ancient Roman road map, consists of eleven parchment sheets assembled into a strip approximately seven meters long but only a third of a meter ______ seas that separate Europe from Africa and Asia depicted as narrow ribbons.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The Tabula Peutingeriana ... consists of eleven parchment sheets assembled into a strip approximately seven meters long but only a third of a meter high” is a complete main clause. What follows, “the seas that separate Europe from Africa and Asia depicted as narrow ribbons,” is an absolute phrase (a noun plus a participle) with no main verb, so a comma correctly attaches it to the main clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join the main clause to the absolute phrase, which has no main verb; “separate” belongs to a relative clause and “depicted” is a participle.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves “The seas that separate Europe from Africa and Asia depicted as narrow ribbons” as a fragment with no main verb.

D.why_wrong: “And” would coordinate the main clause with a phrase that has no main verb, so the sentence is ungrammatical.

items.notes: Subject: history (Roman cartography). Band-7 checks: the trailing element is an absolute phrase whose noun has a relative clause with a finite verb (“that separate”), so B and C look like they introduce a clause; the participle “depicted” cannot be read as a finite verb without an object. Menu as 3.24 (absolute) but the “, and” option replaces 3.24's bare comma-and; the run is the whole 45-word sentence.
band7_moves: trailing absolute phrase whose noun carries a relative clause with a finite verb
semicolon and period options look like they start a clause
the deciding check (no main verb) sits 10+ words after the blank

band7.why: 3.24 (62120607) menu exactly; the absolute phrase’s noun has a relative clause with a finite verb (“that separate”), so semicolon and period look as if a clause follows.

items.subtype: No punctuation between two coordinated that-clauses
items.passage: Biologist Andrew Thurber’s team found that the bristly claws of Kiwa puravida, a crab inhabiting deep-sea methane seeps off Costa Rica, harbor dense populations of ______ and that the crab’s rhythmic claw waving may supply these microorganisms, which it consumes, with oxygen and sulfide.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The verb “found” has two objects, joined by “and”: “that the bristly claws ... harbor dense populations of bacteria” and “that the crab’s rhythmic claw waving may supply these microorganisms ... with oxygen and sulfide.” Because there are only two coordinated elements, no punctuation is needed before “and.”

A.why_wrong: No comma is needed between two coordinated that-clauses; the comma wrongly separates the two objects of “found.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate the two that-clauses, neither of which is an independent clause.

D.why_wrong: A colon can't be used here; “and that the crab’s ...” is the second object of “found,” not an explanation of the first.

items.notes: Subject: science (deep-sea biology, Thurber and colleagues 2011, from recall). Plan asked band 7, but S4_compound has no band-7 official items (band7/boundaries.md, appendix), so it is written as a strong band 6 and band_target is 6: the first that-clause is long and holds a comma-set appositive, so a balancing comma before “and that” looks natural (3.3's move with that-clauses; 2.23's “and the fact that”).

review.note: Comma before “and that” (A) kept as a wrong option: it neither separates independent clauses nor prevents a misreading, so its only defence is a style preference for long coordinates; College Board keys the same comma wrong in 6ea8c23f (3.3, “regions,”) and states that two coordinates take no punctuation. Thurber: Kiwa puravida bacterial farming by claw waving is his team’s published finding; kept.

band7.why: S4_compound has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on 3.3 (6ea8c23f): the long first that-clause with its appositive pair makes the comma before “and that” tempting.

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: When philosopher Antanas Mockus became mayor of Bogotá, Colombia, in 1995, he tried unusual strategies to tame the city’s chaotic traffic. He hired mime artists to silently mock drivers and pedestrians who disregarded traffic ______ over the next decade, the city’s yearly traffic fatalities fell by about half.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “He hired mime artists to silently mock drivers and pedestrians who disregarded traffic rules” and “over the next decade, the city’s yearly traffic fatalities fell by about half” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

items.notes: Subject: social science (urban policy, Bogotá). Medium: the second clause opens with the short time phrase “over the next decade,” so the bare comma looks like it sets off a phrase (2.5's move). Standard menu (2.2, 2.5).

review.note: Mockus: mime artists in Bogotá traffic are his standard record; kept.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a short prepositional phrase
items.passage: When threatened, the hairy frog of Central Africa can force sharp bones in its hind toes to pierce through its own skin, creating makeshift ______ the claws of other vertebrates, these bony projections lack a protective covering of keratin, the tough protein that forms hair and nails.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “When threatened, the hairy frog ... can force sharp bones ... to pierce through its own skin, creating makeshift claws” is a complete sentence. “Unlike the claws of other vertebrates” describes “these bony projections,” the subject of the next sentence, so a period after “claws” is needed.

B.why_wrong: The comma makes “unlike the claws of other vertebrates” look like part of the first sentence, but “these bony projections lack ...” is a second independent clause, so the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, the two independent clauses run together, and “claws unlike the claws of other vertebrates” garbles the first one.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma before it, “and” can't be used to join these two independent clauses.

items.notes: Subject: science (amphibian anatomy). Medium: a 5-word opener before clause 2's subject (2.7's “According to some historians,” and 2.27's “Prior to VisiCalc's release,”). No semicolon option. Facts as reported in 2008 (claws that pierce the skin and lack a keratin sheath); no researcher named.

items.subtype: Comma closing an appositive opened by a comma
items.passage: Filipino director Kidlat Tahimik made Perfumed Nightmare (1977) on a tiny budget, casting himself as the protagonist. His character, a jeepney driver who adores the American space ______ travels to Paris and grows disillusioned with Western promises of technological progress.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The appositive “a jeepney driver who adores the American space program” renames “His character” and is set off from the rest of the sentence. It opens with a comma after “character,” so it must close with a comma after “program” before the verb “travels.”

A.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the appositive opened by the comma after “character” is left unclosed.

C.why_wrong: A dash can't close an appositive that was opened with a comma.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate the subject “His character” from its verb “travels.”

items.notes: Subject: arts (Philippine cinema). Partner comma 11 words before the blank. Architecture differs from w1b3_15 (an appositive on the protagonist, not a title after “first feature”).

review.note: Tahimik: Perfumed Nightmare plot as made; kept.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: Malian writer Amadou Hampâté Bâ devoted decades to recording the oral histories and epics of the Fulani and Bambara peoples. Addressing UNESCO in 1960, he compared the death of an elder to the burning of a ______ the organization to help preserve such traditions before they disappeared.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Addressing UNESCO in 1960, he compared the death of an elder to the burning of a library” is a complete main clause. “Urging the organization to help preserve such traditions ...” is a participial phrase that describes what Bâ was doing as he spoke, so a comma correctly separates it from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join the main clause to “urging the organization ...,” which is a phrase, not an independent clause.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “Urging the organization to help preserve such traditions before they disappeared” as a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “a library urging the organization” wrongly makes the library the one doing the urging; a comma must separate the main clause from the participial phrase.

items.notes: Subject: literature (West African oral tradition). Medium on 2.4 and 2.26 (trailing -ing phrase). Bâ's 1960 UNESCO remark is reported indirectly rather than quoted, since its English wording varies.

review.note: Hampâté Bâ: the library remark at UNESCO in 1960 is his standard record; kept.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject (ending in a relative clause) and its verb
items.passage: In 2019, biologist Sidney Tamm reported that, unlike the permanent anus of most animals with a complete digestive tract, the opening through which the comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi expels undigested ______ appears only when the animal is about to excrete waste and then disappears until it is needed again.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the that-clause is “the opening through which the comb jelly Mnemiopsis leidyi expels undigested food,” and its verb is “appears.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb, however long the subject is.

A.why_wrong: A comma can't separate the subject “the opening ... undigested food” from its verb “appears.”

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate a subject from its verb.

C.why_wrong: A colon can't separate a subject from its verb.

items.notes: Subject: science (invertebrate anatomy; Sidney Tamm's 2019 report on the comb jelly's transient anus, from recall). Medium: a 12-word subject whose relative clause ends at the blank, after a comma-set “unlike” phrase, so a comma feels natural (2.11's move).

review.note: Tamm: 2019 report of the comb jelly’s transient anus is his published finding; kept.

items.subtype: No punctuation between the two parts of a both ... and compound
items.passage: Nigerian photographer J.D. ’Okhai Ojeikere’s Hairstyles series, begun in 1968 and later numbering nearly 1,000 photographs, documents both the elaborate braided and threaded styles that women wore to weddings and other ______ and the simpler ones that they wore to work each day.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Both ... and” joins two noun phrases that serve as objects of “documents”: “the elaborate braided and threaded styles that women wore to weddings and other celebrations” and “the simpler ones that they wore to work each day.” With only two coordinated elements, no punctuation belongs before “and.”

B.why_wrong: No comma is needed between the two parts of the compound joined by “both ... and.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon can't separate two noun phrases that together form the object of “documents.”

D.why_wrong: A colon can't separate the two parts of a compound object; “and the simpler ones ...” does not explain what comes before it.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Nigerian photography). Medium S4_compound (2.23): the first conjunct is long and holds its own “and,” so a comma before the second “and” looks natural. Name written “J.D.” as the photographer is usually credited.

review.note: Ojeikere: Hairstyles series from 1968, nearly 1,000 photographs; kept.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: In the Peruvian Amazon, the Shanay-Timpishka River reaches temperatures high enough to kill small animals that fall in. Although the nearest active volcano is hundreds of kilometers away, the river is heated ______ groundwater rising along deep fractures in Earth’s crust.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “the river is heated by groundwater rising along deep fractures in Earth’s crust,” “groundwater” is the object of the preposition “by.” No punctuation should come between a preposition and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon can't separate the preposition “by” from its object.

B.why_wrong: A comma can't separate the preposition “by” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash can't separate the preposition “by” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: science (geology and hydrology, Peruvian Amazon). Preposition not yet used by our S4_object items.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its object
items.passage: Every year at the end of the rainy season, Wodaabe herders in Niger and Chad gather for the Gerewol, a weeklong celebration. Young men decorate their faces with pigments, adorn themselves with beaded ornaments, and perform elaborate dances while young women watch and ______ the dancers they consider most attractive.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “young women watch and choose the dancers they consider most attractive,” “the dancers” is the object of the verb “choose.” No punctuation should come between a verb and its object.

A.why_wrong: A colon can't separate the verb “choose” from its object.

C.why_wrong: A comma can't separate the verb “choose” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash can't separate the verb “choose” from its object.

items.notes: Subject: social science (anthropology, Sahel pastoralists).

items.subtype: Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Desert locusts usually avoid one another, but crowding can make them swarm. In 2009, researchers linked this transformation to the chemical ______ solitary locusts injected with it began to act like swarming ones.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In 2009, researchers linked this transformation to the chemical serotonin” and “solitary locusts injected with it began to act like swarming ones” are both independent clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

D.why_wrong: No comma belongs after “and” here; nothing is set off between “and” and the subject “solitary locusts.”

items.notes: Subject: science (insect behavior and neurochemistry; the 2009 serotonin finding, researchers unnamed). No bare “serotonin and” option: with clauses this short, a comma-less “and” could be defended (b1 note on w2b1_21).

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: Venezuelan artist Carlos Cruz-Diez treated color as an experience rather than a permanent property of objects. Because the narrow stripes in his Physichromie series appear to shift in color as spectators walk past ______ the works never look identical twice.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Because the narrow stripes ... appear to shift in color as spectators walk past them” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause “the works never look identical twice.” A comma after “them” correctly separates the introductory clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: A comma is needed to mark the end of the introductory dependent clause before the main clause begins.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join a dependent clause to a main clause.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves the dependent clause beginning “Because” as a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Latin American kinetic and op art).

review.note: Cruz-Diez: Physichromie series as described; kept.

items.subtype: Direct question after a question word: inverted order and question mark
items.passage: Thousands of massive stone jars, some considerably taller than an adult, are distributed across the Plain of Jars in northern Laos. What ______ Because human remains and burial pits have been discovered nearby, most archaeologists believe the jars served a funerary purpose.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “What” begins a direct question, so the subject and the helping verb are inverted (“were the jars used for”) and the sentence ends with a question mark. The next sentence then answers the question.

A.why_wrong: A direct question beginning with “What” needs inverted word order (“were the jars”), not statement order.

C.why_wrong: Statement order with a period leaves “What the jars were used for” as a fragment rather than a question.

D.why_wrong: The word order is correct for a direct question, but a direct question must end with a question mark, not a period.

items.notes: Subject: history (archaeology, Laos). Direct form (1.18, 1.30), since b1's question item was embedded.

items.subtype: Comma before a sentence-final nonrestrictive which clause
items.passage: From about 2500 to 1500 BCE, Kerma, a city on the Nile in present-day Sudan, was the capital of a powerful kingdom. At its center stood a monumental mud-brick temple now known as the Western ______ still rises approximately 18 meters above the surrounding landscape.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “At its center stood a monumental mud-brick temple now known as the Western Deffufa” is a complete main clause. The clause “which still rises approximately 18 meters ...” adds information about a temple already identified by name, so it is nonrestrictive and must be set off with a comma.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon can't join the main clause to the relative clause beginning with “which,” which is not an independent clause.

B.why_wrong: The period leaves “Which still rises approximately 18 meters above the surrounding landscape” as a fragment.

D.why_wrong: A relative clause that adds information about a named structure is nonrestrictive and needs a comma before “which.”

items.notes: Subject: history (ancient Sudan). Kept clear of “Nubian” wording used in w1b2_09.

items.subtype: Semicolon between independent clauses
items.passage: Kaurna, the language of the Aboriginal people of South Australia’s Adelaide Plains, had lost its last fluent speakers by the early twentieth ______ since the 1990s, community members and linguists have revived it using vocabularies and a grammar compiled by missionaries in the 1840s.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Kaurna ... had lost its last fluent speakers by the early twentieth century” and “since the 1990s, community members and linguists have revived it ...” are both independent clauses. A semicolon correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: A comma alone can't join two independent clauses.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation or conjunction, the two independent clauses run together.

C.why_wrong: When “and” joins two long independent clauses such as these, a comma is needed before it.

items.notes: Subject: language (Aboriginal language revival, South Australia). Menu of 1.4 (comma, none, “and”). No period option.
